newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya coffee estate starts major replanting scheme.
newsitem.headline: Kenya coffee estate starts major replanting scheme.

text.p: One of Kenya's biggest coffee estates has started a major replanting scheme to replace all coffee trees in an entire area of 15,000 acres in a project that will take 10 years, its leaders said.

Peder Mortensen, managing director of the Standard Chartered Estate Management, whose clients produce about 15 percent of Kenya's total coffee output, said the estate had launched a commercial plant nursery earlier this month.

Mortensen, speaking to Reuters in the central highlands of Thika, 60 km north of Nairobi, said the entire area would be replanted with Ruiru 11 -- a locally-developed, disease-resistant and cost-reducing variety which is expected to increase yields by at least 25 percent.

"We have just set up a commercial nursery at the beginning of March which will be producing 1.5 million seedlings a year. That's enough to convert all our 15,000 acres into Ruiru 11 within 10 years," he told Reuters on Thursday.
"With Ruiru 11 we are saving 30 percent of production costs for not having to spray chemicals against coffee berry disease."
The Standard Chartered estate comprises 67 plantations which produce average yields of 1.8 tonnes per hectare, significantly higher than the national Kenyan average of some 500 kg per hectare.
Mortensen, a Dane involved in Kenya's coffee industry since 1954, said the estate had replanted 375 acres with Ruiru 11 over the past five years and results were encouraging.

"We have definitively been getting better yields with the new variety, an increase of about 25 percent. But yields could be a lot more than that, it's still too early after just five years to say whether 25 percent is the average," he said.
He said in areas of the estate where coffee trees were not affected with CBD, part responsible for a downward forecast in 1996/97 production, yields had been as high as 3.6 tonnes.
The Ruiru 11 is a hybrid of the catimore variety, the traditional Kenyan SL variety and Rume Sudan -- making up 70 percent, 25 percent and five percent of Ruiru 11 respectively.
The catimore is itself a hybrid of the Indonesian Timor variety and the Caturra from South America and is a dwarf-type arabica coffee which has led to successful crops around the world.

The Catimore produces high yields, is resistant to rust-leave disease, can be grown at high density rates and matures to full-producing trees in just three years. The Rume Sudan is known to be resistant to CBD.
The Ruiru 11 has been controversial with industry critics saying it reduced the quality of Kenya's world-famous coffee.
Mortensen said if Kenya were to increase production figures higher yields were of vital importance, and that could only be reached through varieties resistant to CBD.
"With Ruiru 11 we are reducing costs by 30 percent and increasing yields by at least 25 percent, while at the same time maintaining acceptable quality," he told Reuters.
"We are definitively recommending replanting (of Kenya's coffee plantations) with CBD-resistant varieties because CBD is the biggest pest and the biggest yield-eliminating factor."

He forecast production at the estate in the 1996/97 crop year would slump by 14.5 percent to 10,000 tonnes, down from 11,700 tonnes in the 1995/96 season, mostly due to a drought which has swept through East Africa, but in part due to CBD.
